375467a093490920e992ffa0c494dd9e.text: A fall storm will bring mixed weather conditions to the multiple B.C. regions on Saturday, Oct. 17, according to Environment Canada. A little bit of nearly every kind of weather is expected on Saturday, Oct. 17 in the Eastern Fraser Valley, Okanagan, and Cariboo regions, including the Coquihalla Highway (Hope to Kamloops), Okanagan Connector, and Highway 3 (Hope to Princeton via Allison Pass), prompting Environment Canada to issue a special weather statement on Friday morning. The only area not impacted is the Chilcotin area, including Kamloops and Ashcroft. According to the government weather agency, a fall storm is going to bring mixed weather conditions, including heavy winds. “A sharp cold front moving across the B.C. Interior on Saturday will primarily generate strong gusty winds of 60 to 80 km/h,” stated Environment Canada. “Ahead of this cold front, strong southwest winds gusting to 80 km/h will develop lee of the Coast Mountains in the Chilcotin this morning.” Additionally, the cold front and unstable air could generate scattered showers, small hail and risk of thunderstorms across the central interior and parts of the Columbia regions. The weather could result in localized power outages, fallen branches, slippery conditions for drivers. High profile vehicles should also take caution in the high winds, added Environment Canada.

d6f7103a27358f395185ad968c97c674.text: The Kelowna RCMP is alerting the public to an ongoing telephone scam following an increase in reports involving fraudsters who are spoofing the detachment's non-emergency phone number, 250-762-3300. Individuals across Canada are receiving calls from someone alleging to be an RCMP officer, and the number appears to originate from the Kelowna detachment’s legitimate non-emergency line. These calls are a phone scam, where the fraudster appears genuinely connected to the Kelowna RCMP, in order to deceive individuals into providing sensitive personal and financial information. After receiving a significant number of reports from people claiming to have received fraudulent calls from the Kelowna RCMP non-emergency line, police are alerting the public to an ongoing scam involving fraudsters spoofing the detachment’s non-emergency phone number, 250-762-3300. According to Cpl. Allison Konsmo, the fraudulent caller falsely identifies themselves as an RCMP officer and claims police have a person in custody who is allegedly in possession of their personal information. “The caller then attempts to persuade the victim to click on a link and provide sensitive information, including passwords, account details, and other personal information,” said Cpl. Konsmo. • Request that you provide financial information to secure your accounts. “These calls are not originating from the Kelowna RCMP, despite what may appear on caller ID,” said Cpl. Konsmo. “We want to remind the public that caller ID information can be manipulated and should not be relied upon as proof of who is calling.” Anyone who receives one of these calls is encouraged to hang up immediately and avoid engaging with the caller. If you are unsure whether a call from police is legitimate, disconnect and contact your local police agency using a publicly listed phone number. If you are a victim of fraud, please contact the Kelowna RCMP non-emergency line at 250-762-3300. For more information on fraud or to report an incident

In communities across British Columbia, sport is about much more than competition. It’s where children build friendships, volunteers bring neighbours together, and families gather at local arenas, fields, pools and recreation centres. But for too many families, particularly in smaller and rural communities, the opportunity to participate is becoming increasingly difficult to afford. As British Columbians prepare to vote in municipal and provincial elections, affordability is understandably dominating the conversation. Yet one important consideration risks being overlooked: whether families can afford to keep their children involved in sport, and whether their communities have the facilities and resources to make participation possible. In many parts of regional B.C., the challenges are particularly acute. A young hockey player may have to travel hours for games or practices. A family whose child participates in swimming, soccer or basketball may face significant transportation and accommodation costs simply because local programs or facilities are unavailable. Registration fees, equipment and tournament expenses add to the financial pressure. For families with more than one child, those costs can quickly become overwhelming. And while larger centres may offer multiple facilities and programs, smaller communities often depend on a single arena, aging recreation centre or limited number of playing fields. When facilities require major repairs, or programs cannot attract enough coaches and volunteers, opportunities can disappear. These are not simply recreation issues. They are questions of affordability, community health and the future of smaller communities. Sport BC believes the next provincial government, along with newly elected municipal councils, has an important opportunity to address these challenges. CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko said, during a visit to Langley on Friday, Oct. 16, that her party would provide permanent spaces for 25,000 more students in B.C. public schools. She said the new classroom spaces will be in place by 2031, with the districts with the most portables and fastest growth targeted first. “We’ll keep class size and class composition limits in teachers contacts and fund them fully,” Sturko said. Among her promises was to bring back letter grades for students from Grade 4 and up, to give a clear picture of student progress to parents. She also promised to add 1,500 education assistants to B.C. classrooms, fund behaviour support teams in every district, and bring in 350 child- and youth-care workers and behaviour specialists. Sturko also said school food programs would expand to 40 per cent of B.C. students by 2030. The CentreBC leader also pledged more school counsellors, and extending early reading screening-style programs to math as well. She said her party could pay for their educational plan while returning the province’s books to balance. “Unlike the other parties, we actually have a path to balance in two terms,” she said, calling the incumbent NDP government’s deficit spending a “payday loan.” Joining Sturko Friday were four of her regional candidates – Kyle Stevenson from Langley-Walnut Grove, Parm Bhandol from Surrey North, Paul Brar from Surrey-Fleetwood, and Sargy Chima from Surrey-Cloverdale. Langley and Surrey have seen rapid growth of young families, and have disproportionately seen portable classrooms sprout up outside schools. It was all hands on deck at the Williams Lake Boys Girls Club on Friday, Oct. 16 as the not-for-profit society serving local children and youth got ready to welcome families to their annual haunted house. Iconic Horror is the theme of this year’s event set to provide good scares in addition to popcorn and burgers cooked up by Cariboo Chevrolet Buick GMC Ltd. “We do it for the community,” said regional director of community engagement and fund development Krista Harvey. “It’s something to bring people together and the haunted house is always great. It’s not for everyone because it can be scary but it’s just one way to bring the community together and do something for the community just like our street party.” Independent living coordinator Brooke Hill served as this year’s event planner. She selected the theme based on movies she liked watching growing up that scared her, and believes there is a frightful movie for every generation. “This is my first year independently doing the haunted house, so I’m really nervous,” Hill said, adding everyone had so much fun last year. Planning for the haunted house gets started in July followed by many meetings and securing volunteers in the weeks leading up to getting the club located downtown across from FreshCo transformed. The by-donation event supports programs offered by the club. “We serve a lot of youth in this community every day,” Hill noted. After Friday’s family-friendly evening the Williams Lake Boys Girls Club is ready to provide full-on scares Saturday, Oct. 17 from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.

A notice on the Village of Valemount website said the Saturday, Oct. 17 municipal election was cancelled because all candidates for mayor and the four council seats had been elected by acclamation. On his X bio, the 1977-born Torgerson refers to himself as “On Leave Mayor of Valemount.” Under the NDP government’s amendments to the Community Charter, a member of a council is under mandatory leave of absence if charged under the Criminal Code “for a period that begins on the date of the charge, and ends” the day after the acquittal, discharge or withdrawal of the charge or on the date of conviction. b7b0a06ab29c42c7b933233264bd615f.text: Jenifer Kosman is calling on Canada Post to bring back Forest Grove's post office. Members of the Forest Grove community are looking for a new post office after it closed earlier this year. The post office closed at the end of January this year, following the postmaster’s retirement. At the time, Canada Post described the closure as temporary, pending the hiring of a new postmaster. However, almost nine months later, the post office remains shuttered, and the mailboxes have been removed. Since the closure, Forest Grove residents like Jenifer Kosman have had to drive at least 15 minutes into town to pick up their mail from the 100 Mile House Post Office. As a small business owner who relies on the mail to deliver her hand-sewn products, Kosman said the lack of a local post office is more than just an inconvenience. “It’s frustrating because once our post master had gone and retired on us, that kind of left us with nothing. We have a couple of buildings in the area that are possibilities,” Kosman said. “I have heard the (Forest Grove Store) may be interested in putting it back in with them.” Kosman said she has heard from other Forest Grove residents that Canada Post is reluctant to use these possible locations due to the buildings’ age. She noted she has heard there was a bathroom and water issue in the old building that hosted the former post office. When reached for comment, Phil Legault of Canada Post’s media relations said that the postal service is still looking for a suitable location that meets its requirements, noting that this is a “postmaster-provided post office.” While Kosman believes Canada Post has hired a new postmaster for Forest Grove, however, Legault’s comment on the matter was that Canada Post had begun the hiring process to find a replacement. “What we can provide as an update is that we continue to work diligently to resume consistent postal services in the community,” Legault said. “As we have more information, we will share it with local

31de31f15bc2e21e766029cd1d48c5c2.text: *100 Mile Free Press columnist Ken Alexander interviewed the two candidates running for the Thompson-Nicola Regional District’s Area E, incumbent Jim Smith and Challenger Sally Watson. Voting day is this Saturday, Oct. 17.* Sally Watson wants to become the next Area E Director for the Thompson-Nicola Regional District. She also wants to see changes for the Seventy Mile Access Centre (SMAC). Watson noted that the elementary school building where SMAC is now was closed in 2000 and was inspected in 2008, and it would take $500,000 to fix it. She explained that the only way to fund this would be by creating the Specified Taxation area and by billing all the taxpayers for the upgrade. Watson claimed the current Area E Director, Jim Smith, talked to the SMAC board and told them he and the TNRD were working on a situation where the TNRD would acquire the building and SMAC could use it for $1 per year. Furthermore, the TNRD would do the repairs. There is no doubt that the School District wants to get rid of the property as there is no room in their budget for demolition, she added. Watson is concerned that the SMAC executives were told to keep this quiet and that Director Smith isn’t explaining the difficulty of finding the money for the job, she said. The Canadian Community Building Fund allotment for Area E is about $54,000.00 per year, she added.
